name: Budibud
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only documentation is a short 1892 wordlist (J. P. Thomson); no grammar or phonology exists.

new_statements.quote: Stress is phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima, and probably also in Nimowa and Sud-Est. Stress is not indicated in any practical orthography. In all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs. When a kinship noun is pluralised by the addition of a suffix, the stress moves one syllable closer to the end of the word. In Muyuw the stress moves in the same way, though no suffix is added. When an intransitive verb is made transitive, an object suffix is usually added, and the stress moves one syllable closer to the end of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic) in Budibud and no positional rule is given; it is said to be predictable only within certain word-classes (kinship nouns, verbs), where affixation moves it one syllable toward the end of the word. Budibud examples (p. 466): tʌ́wan 'his older brother', bwʌ́dan 'his younger brother' (stress on the first syllable), ikatúnag 'he gets ready' (intr.) vs ikatinɛ́gɛ-n 'he gets it ready' (trans.), i.e. stress shifts rightward when the object suffix is added.
new_statements.exceptions: Internal tension in the source: p. 475 says kinship-noun plural suffixation shifts stress in all PTC languages, but p. 466 says of the same family 'In Muyuw the plural is marked by change of stress, while the suffix -s is added in Budibud with no change of stress' (tʌ́wan / tʌ́wans). Lithgow also notes a separate, non-stress pattern of vowel lengthening near the end of the phonological word (penult in Dobu, final in Muyuw); nothing said about Budibud length.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (citation forms and inflected verb/noun forms from Lithgow's own SIL survey data). The statement is an areal one covering the Kilivila family/Papuan Tip cluster with Budibud named explicitly; it is a survey chapter, not a dedicated Budibud phonology, and the stress-marked Budibud forms on p. 466 are the only first-hand Budibud data.
new_statements.identity_note: Lithgow 1976 lists the language as 'Budibud (Nada)', 'spoken only on the Laughlan Islands' (p. 452) = budi1249; the older sources (Thomson 1892, Ray 1907) call it Nada. The stress statement on p. 475 is made jointly for Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud and Misima (Papuan Tip cluster); the Budibud-specific evidence is the stress-marked kinship-noun and verb forms on p. 466. No dialects are distinguished.

sources.note: Sec. 84 'Stress' (p. 475): stress is phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima; not marked in orthographies; predictable only within certain word-classes (kinship nouns, verbs) where it shifts one syllable rightward under suffixation. P. 466 gives Budibud examples with stress marked: tʌ́wan 'his older brother' / tʌ́wans 'his older brothers' (plural -s added 'with no change of stress', unlike Muyuw túwan/tuwán); ikatúnag 'he gets ready (intr.)' vs ikatinɛ́gɛ-n 'he gets it ready (trans.)'. Budibud is listed as 'Budibud (Nada)', spoken only on the Laughlan Islands (p. 452).
